## Problem

When a user @mentions the Hermes bot in an existing Discord thread for the first time, the bot starts a brand-new session with no awareness of the prior conversation in that thread. This produces a poor user experience — the bot responds as if the thread history doesn't exist.

The Slack adapter already handles this correctly via `_fetch_thread_context()` (added in #5890), but the Discord adapter has no equivalent.

## Expected behavior

When the bot is first @mentioned in a Discord thread (no existing session), it should fetch the thread's prior messages via the Discord API and inject them as context, so the agent can respond with full awareness of the ongoing conversation.

## Implementation

Ports the same pattern from the Slack adapter (`_fetch_thread_context` + `_has_active_session_for_thread`) to the Discord adapter:

- `_has_active_session_for_thread()` — checks the session store using `build_session_key()` (respects `thread_sessions_per_user` / `group_sessions_per_user` settings)
- `_fetch_thread_context()` — fetches up to 30 prior messages from the thread via `channel.history()`, formats them as `[Thread context] ... [End of thread context]`, skipping bot messages and the current trigger message
- Injection in `_handle_message` — only triggers for existing threads (not auto-created ones) when there's no prior session, prepending context to the event text

items.title: [Feature]: Add ACP session token counts and cost data in state.db

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Problem                                                   
                                                                                
  When using the ACP (Agent Client Protocol) for editor/GUI integrations,       
  sessions are persisted to state.db with zero token counts and no cost data.   
  This makes it impossible for client applications to display accurate usage    
  metrics or aggregate cost tracking for ACP sessions.      

  We discovered this while building https://github.com/awizemann/scarf, a native
   macOS GUI for Hermes. Our dashboard, insights, and session browser all
  aggregate cost and token data from state.db -- but ACP sessions contribute    
  nothing because the fields are never populated.           

  Verified directly against the DB:                                             
  -- CLI sessions: tokens and cost populated correctly
  SELECT id, source, estimated_cost_usd, input_tokens, output_tokens FROM       
  sessions                                                                      
  WHERE source = 'cli' ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 3;                        
  -- 20260409_013053_13d0fc | cli | 0.1471952 | 7660  | 6171                    
  -- 20260409_012654_523168 | cli | 0.1341210 | 4486  | 5136                    
  -- 20260409_012202_138f65 | cli | 0.1339732 | 10433 | 9853                    
                                                                                
  -- ACP sessions: all zeros                                                    
  SELECT id, source, estimated_cost_usd, input_tokens, output_tokens FROM       
  sessions                                                                      
  WHERE source = 'acp' ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 3;    
  -- 49bb19ef-... | acp | NULL | 0 | 0                  
  -- 2a5ffe54-... | acp | NULL | 0 | 0
  -- f114d932-... | acp | NULL | 0 | 0                                          
                                                                                
  Root cause: acp_adapter/session.py _persist() writes messages via             
  db.append_message() but never updates input_tokens, output_tokens,            
  reasoning_tokens, estimated_cost_usd, or related fields on the session record.
   The PromptResponse returned by server.py includes a Usage object with token  
  counts, but these are only sent back to the client over the wire -- they're
  never written to the DB.

  By contrast, CLI sessions get their token/cost fields populated by the agent's
   run() method, which calls the cost calculation logic after each turn.
                                                                                
  Impact                                                    

  - Cost tracking is blind to ACP usage. Any dashboard, analytics, or billing   
  view that aggregates from state.db will undercount by the entire ACP usage.
  - Session browser shows incomplete data. ACP sessions appear with 0 tokens and
   no cost, making them look like empty sessions.                               
  - No way to reconstruct from the client side. The ACP PromptResponse returns
  token counts but not cost, and clients don't have access to provider pricing  
  tables to compute cost themselves.                       

### Proposed Solution

After each prompt completion in the ACP server, update the session record in  
  state.db with cumulative token counts and estimated cost. Two changes needed:
                                                                                
  1. Accumulate and persist token totals                                        
  
  In acp_adapter/session.py, after _persist() writes messages, also update the  
  session's token columns. The Usage object from the PromptResponse already has
  the per-turn token counts -- accumulate them on the SessionState and write    
  them to the DB:                                           

  # In SessionState dataclass, add accumulators:
  total_input_tokens: int = 0
  total_output_tokens: int = 0
  total_reasoning_tokens: int = 0                                               
  total_cache_read_tokens: int = 0
  total_cache_write_tokens: int = 0                                             
                                                            
  # After prompt completion in server.py, accumulate:                           
  state.total_input_tokens += usage.input_tokens
  state.total_output_tokens += usage.output_tokens                              
  # ... etc                                                 
                                                                                
  # In _persist(), update the session record:
  db._conn.execute(                                                             
      """UPDATE sessions SET                                
         input_tokens = ?, output_tokens = ?, reasoning_tokens = ?,             
         cache_read_tokens = ?, cache_write_tokens = ?
         WHERE id = ?""",                                                       
      (state.total_input_tokens, state.total_output_tokens, ...)
  )                                                                             
                                                            
  2. Compute and persist estimated cost                                         
  
  Reuse the same cost estimation logic that CLI sessions use (likely in         
  hermes_cli or the billing module) to compute estimated_cost_usd based on the
  model, provider, and token counts. Write it to the session record alongside   
  the token totals.                                         

  If the cost calculation is tightly coupled to the CLI agent's run() loop, an  
  alternative is to expose it as a utility function that the ACP adapter can
  call after each prompt.                                                       
                                                            
  3. (Optional) Include cost in PromptResponse

  For clients that want real-time cost display without polling the DB, include  
  estimated_cost_usd in the PromptResponse alongside the existing Usage fields:
                                                                                
  return PromptResponse(                                    
      stop_reason=stop_reason,
      usage=usage,                                                              
      # New field:
      estimated_cost_usd=computed_cost,                                         
  )                                                                             
  
  ---                                                                           
  This would make ACP sessions first-class citizens in the Hermes data model,
  with the same token/cost visibility that CLI and cron sessions already have.  
 

### Alternatives Considered

_No response_

### Feature Type

Other

### Scope

Small (single file, < 50 lines)

items.title: [Feature]: auxiliary_client.py should honor api_mode flag (parallel to runtime_provider.py)
items.body:
## Problem

`hermes_cli/runtime_provider.py` supports an `api_mode` flag in `config.yaml` (`chat_completions` / `codex_responses` / `anthropic_messages`) and also has URL-based auto-detection (`_detect_api_mode_for_url` at line 36) that maps `api.openai.com` → `codex_responses`.

But `agent/auxiliary_client.py` — which handles `auxiliary.*`, `compression.*`, and `delegation` resolution — is a completely parallel chain that **ignores `api_mode` entirely**. It calls `client.chat.completions.create(**kwargs)` directly, with no way to route through `/v1/responses`.

This breaks using codex-family models for auxiliary tasks on a standard `OPENAI_API_KEY`. If you set:

```yaml
auxiliary:
  compression:
    model: gpt-5.3-codex
    base_url: https://api.openai.com/v1
    api_mode: codex_responses   # ← silently ignored
```

the call still hits `/v1/chat/completions` and 404s with *"This is not a chat model and thus not supported in the v1/chat/completions endpoint"*.

## Related

- #6209 — custom endpoint setup should expose `api_mode` in the CLI wizard. Same underlying family of gap, but #6209 is about the `runtime_provider.py` path (main chat). This issue is about the `auxiliary_client.py` path being a separate, parallel system that also needs the flag.
- The existing `_try_codex()` function in `auxiliary_client.py` (around line 900) does route through the Responses API via `CodexAuxiliaryClient`, but only for ChatGPT OAuth auth — not for standard `OPENAI_API_KEY` + `api.openai.com`.

## Proposed Solution

Two options:

**Option A — Honor `api_mode` in `auxiliary_client.py`.** When resolving a custom endpoint, check the `api_mode` field and use `CodexAuxiliaryClient` (the existing Responses API adapter) instead of a raw chat-completions client. The adapter already handles content translation via `_convert_content_for_responses`, so wiring it up for the non-OAuth API-key case should be localized.

**Option B — Unify the two resolution systems.** Collapse `auxiliary_client.py` into `runtime_provider.py` so there's one `api_mode`-aware path for everything. Bigger refactor but eliminates the confusing split.

I'd lean toward Option A as the minimal fix.

## Use Case

Discovered during live debugging on a ChatGPT Team plan. When the weekly Codex quota blew, I wanted all Hermes-side tasks (not just main chat) to fall through to `gpt-5.3-codex` on my pay-per-token API key instead of degrading to `gpt-5.4-mini`. The `fallback_model` path works (via `api_mode: codex_responses` per #6209's underlying functionality); the auxiliary path is the remaining gap.

## Scope

- `agent/auxiliary_client.py` — resolution chain, approximately lines 900-1000
- No changes to `runtime_provider.py` or the CLI wizard
- Add a note to `website/docs/developer-guide/provider-runtime.md` about both resolution systems honoring `api_mode`

Happy to submit a PR for Option A if maintainers agree on the approach.

- Both are llama.cpp servers on separate A100-80GB GPUs

## Config (`~/.hermes/config.yaml` delegation section)
```yaml
delegation:
  model: Qwopus-MoE-35B-A3B-Q8_0
  provider: ''
  base_url: http://localhost:8000/v1
  api_key: local
  max_iterations: 150
  default_toolsets:
  - terminal
  - file
```

## Debug output
Added print statements at three points in `tools/delegate_tool.py`:

```
# Point 1: inside _resolve_delegation_credentials(), after reading config
DEBUG delegation: base_url='http://localhost:8000/v1' api_key='local' model='Qwopus-MoE-35B-A3B-Q8_0'

# Point 2: inside _build_child_agent(), at effective_base_url assignment
DEBUG build_child: override_base_url='http://localhost:8000/v1' parent_base_url='http://localhost:8001/v1'

# Point 3: just before AIAgent() constructor call
DEBUG AIAgent call: effective_base_url='http://localhost:8000/v1' effective_provider='custom' effective_api_key='local'
```

All three points show the correct `:8000` endpoint. However, session DB records for child
sessions show `billing_base_url: http://localhost:8001/v1` — meaning `self.base_url` is `:8001`
at the time of the actual API call inside `run_conversation()`.

## Evidence
Child session records from `SessionDB.list_sessions_rich(include_children=True)`:
```
# Child sessions (parent_session_id is set) all show wrong billing_base_url
20260409_220841 parent=20260409_220822  billing_base_url=http://localhost:8001/v1  model=Qwopus-MoE-35B-A3B-Q8_0
20260409_220437 parent=20260409_220423  billing_base_url=http://localhost:8001/v1  model=Qwopus-MoE-35B-A3B-Q8_0
```

Note: model name is correctly `Qwopus` (from delegation config) but base_url is wrong (parent's).

Also confirmed via llama-server logs: `:8000` receives `POST /api/show` (model probe) but never
`POST /v1/chat/completions` — meaning the child agent probes the right endpoint for model
metadata but sends actual completions to the parent's endpoint.

## Root cause hypothesis
Something inside `AIAgent.__init__()` overwrites `base_url` after receiving it as a parameter.
The `billing_base_url` is set from `self.base_url` at line 7972 of `run_agent.py`, so the
overwrite happens between construction and the first API call. Likely candidates:
- Provider resolution re-running inside `__init__` and inheriting parent context
- `_primary_runtime` snapshot capturing wrong state
- `resolve_runtime_provider()` call inside `__init__` overriding the passed `base_url`

## Additional notes
- `delegation.base_url` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (global) is required — putting it only in a
  profile's `config.yaml` does not work because `_load_config()` in `delegate_tool.py` reads
  `CLI_CONFIG` first, which is populated from `load_cli_config()` in `cli.py`, which reads
  `_hermes_home / config.yaml` (always the global config regardless of active profile).
- The issue only affects `base_url` routing — model name from delegation config is correctly
  applied to child sessions.
- Workaround: use the coder profile directly instead of relying on delegation routing.

items.title: [Bug] Telegram /background can interrupt an active run instead of starting a background task
items.body:
## Summary

In Telegram, `/background <prompt>` does not consistently behave like a side-task command when the main session is already busy. Instead of starting a separate background task, it can interrupt the active conversation and feed the literal slash command back through the interrupt path.

## Reproduction

1. Start a long-running task in a Telegram chat with Hermes.
2. While that task is still running, send a message like:
   ```
   /background check out the new allium mcp https://docs.allium.so/ai/mcp/overview https://agents.allium.so set it up with our api key instead of doing the existing way we're using allium
   ```
3. Observe that Hermes may interrupt the active run instead of cleanly launching the background task.

## Expected behavior

`/background` should behave like a side-channel command even while the main run is active:
- it should start a separate background task
- it should not interrupt the active conversation
- it should not be passed through as ordinary interrupt text

## Actual behavior

In Telegram gateway sessions, `/background` can be treated like a normal incoming message during an active run and trigger the active-session interrupt flow. From the user's perspective, this looks like `/background` failed to queue a side task and instead hijacked the main conversation.

## Likely cause

This looks like a gateway busy-session dispatch gap rather than a background-task runner bug. There are two places to check:

1. `gateway/platforms/base.py` active-session guard
   Certain slash commands bypass the active-session guard and are dispatched directly, but `/background` may not be consistently included there.

2. `gateway/run.py` running-agent fast path
   When a session already has a running agent, `/background` appears to fall through to the default interrupt behavior instead of being routed to `_handle_background_command(...)`.

## Scope

Observed in Telegram. This may also affect other gateway platforms that share the same busy-session command dispatch path.

## Notes

Restarting the gateway can clear the current in-memory active session state, but that does not appear to fix the underlying bug. The issue reproduces again on later active runs.

items.title: [Bug]: Slack image attachments can be cached as HTML sign-in pages, causing downstream vision failures
items.body:
## Bug Description

Slack image attachments received through the gateway can be downloaded as a Slack HTML sign-in / redirect page and then cached locally with a `.png`/`.jpg` extension. Hermes later surfaces that cached path to the agent as if it were a real image, but `vision_analyze` eventually rejects it with `Only real image files are supported for vision analysis.`

This turns an upstream Slack media download/auth/access failure into a confusing downstream vision failure.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run Hermes with the Slack gateway enabled.
2. In a Slack channel/thread where Hermes is active, mention the bot and attach an image.
3. Ask Hermes to inspect/read the image (or rely on the normal image-analysis path).
4. In failing cases, inspect the cached file under `~/.hermes/cache/images/` (or legacy `~/.hermes/image_cache/`).
5. Observe that the cached `*.png`/`*.jpg` file is actually HTML, and later `vision_analyze` fails.

Minimal evidence from a real repro:

```shell
$ file /Users/frog/.hermes/image_cache/img_244acf0cbbfe.png
/Users/frog/.hermes/image_cache/img_244acf0cbbfe.png: HTML document text, ASCII text, with very long lines (28115)
```

The cached file begins with `<!DOCTYPE html>` and has `<title>Slack</title>`.

## Expected Behavior

If Slack media download fails or returns HTML / non-image bytes, Hermes should:

- reject the download immediately,
- log a clear Slack download/auth/access error,
- avoid caching the response as an image,
- and avoid handing the agent a bogus local image path.

## Actual Behavior

Hermes caches arbitrary response bytes as an image file and only fails later, when `vision_analyze` performs magic-byte validation and returns:

```shell
Error analyzing image: Only real image files are supported for vision analysis.
```

## Affected Component

- Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)
- Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

- Slack

## Operating System

macOS 13.7.8

## Python Version

3.11.15

## Hermes Version

v0.8.0 (2026.4.8)

## Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell
vision_analyze -> Error analyzing image: Only real image files are supported for vision analysis.

$ file /Users/frog/.hermes/image_cache/img_244acf0cbbfe.png
HTML document text, ASCII text, with very long lines (28115)
```

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)

Current Slack image handling appears to accept the response body as image bytes without validating that it is actually an image:

- `gateway/platforms/slack.py:874-882` routes Slack `image/*` attachments into `_download_slack_file(...)`
- `gateway/platforms/slack.py:1299-1321` performs an authenticated GET and then immediately calls `cache_image_from_bytes(response.content, ext)`
- `gateway/platforms/base.py:95-110` blindly writes those bytes to disk
- `tools/vision_tools.py:102-121` and `355-357` later detect that the cached file is not a real image and reject it

So even if the underlying trigger is Slack auth/scope/access/redirect behavior, Hermes currently converts that upstream failure into a misleading downstream vision error instead of failing at the Slack download boundary.

Related external reports show the same Slack symptom (HTML sign-in page instead of file bytes):

- openclaw/openclaw#18642
- openclaw/openclaw#1936
- slackapi/bolt-python#1283

## Proposed Fix (optional)

1. Validate Slack download responses before caching them as images.
   - Reject `text/html` responses.
   - Also validate image magic bytes (not just extension / Slack metadata) before `cache_image_from_bytes(...)`.
2. Return/log an explicit Slack media download error when the response is HTML or otherwise not an image.
3. Add a regression test that simulates `200 OK` + HTML body from a Slack file URL and asserts Hermes does **not** cache it as an image.

There are already retry-path tests for Slack media download, but I did not find a regression test for the `HTTP 200 but body is HTML login page` case.

items.title: 9 bugs in V4A patch parser and fuzzy match: data loss, partial apply, silent errors

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Overview

Nine confirmed bugs in `tools/patch_parser.py` and `tools/fuzzy_match.py`, grouped by severity.

---

## Tier 1 — Data Loss / Correctness

### Bug 1: Files > 2000 lines silently truncated on UPDATE

`_apply_update` called `read_file(limit=10000)`, but `read_file` clamps the limit to `MAX_LINES = 2000`. For any file longer than 2000 lines, `write_file` overwrites the file with only the first 2000 lines — lines 2001–N are permanently lost.

A second issue in the same path: `_add_line_numbers` truncates lines > 2000 chars with `"... [truncated]"`. Content is then reconstructed from this annotated output, permanently corrupting long lines.

### Bug 2: `apply_v4a_operations` continues after a failure

When operation N fails, operations N+1 … M are still applied. The result reports `success=False` but the filesystem is already partially modified with no rollback.

### Bug 3: `parse_v4a_patch` never returns an error

The function signature promises `Tuple[List[PatchOperation], Optional[str]]`. The second element was always `None`. A begin-marker-with-no-ops, empty file path, or move missing a destination all silently returned `([], None)` — indistinguishable from a legitimately empty patch.

---

## Tier 2 — Incorrect Match Behaviour

### Bug 4: Strategy 7 (block anchor) similarity threshold is 10%

When there is exactly one candidate block, the similarity threshold for middle-section matching was `0.10`. In files with repetitive structure (similar function definitions, boilerplate classes), this silently replaces the wrong block.

### Bug 5: Unicode characters (smart quotes, em-dash) bypass strategies 1–6

`_unicode_normalize` was applied only inside strategy 7 (block anchor). LLM-generated patches with smart quotes or em-dashes fell through to the most permissive fuzzy strategy, risking incorrect matches where exact matches should have succeeded.

### Bug 6: Match strategy not surfaced to caller

`fuzzy_find_and_replace` returned a 3-tuple `(content, count, error)`. When a fuzzy fallback strategy fired, callers had no visibility and could not warn the user that manual verification was warranted.

---

## Tier 3 — Low-Severity Correctness Gaps

### Bug 7: Ambiguous addition-only hunk context hint silently inserts at wrong location

`str.find` returns the first occurrence. If a context hint appears more than once, insertion silently goes to the wrong location with no error.

### Bug 8: `_apply_delete` returned success on missing file

A typo in the file path produced `(True, "# ... already deleted")` — silent success with nothing deleted.

### Bug 9: `_apply_move` had no preconditions

A pre-existing destination was silently overwritten by `mv`. (A missing source produced a non-zero exit which was caught, but only after the call.)

---

Related: #507 (Tier 2 intent overlap — Unicode normalisation §2d, error messages §2e)

items.title: Bug: skills_sync.py uses directory name instead of SKILL.md name field, causing builtin skills misclassified as local
items.body:
## Bug Description

There is an inconsistency in how skill names are handled across different modules, causing 9 official builtin skills to be incorrectly classified as `local` instead of `builtin`.

## Root Cause

Different modules use different methods to identify skills:

| File | Function | Method | Status |
|------|----------|--------|--------|
| `tools/skills_sync.py` | `_discover_bundled_skills()` | Uses **directory name** (`skill_dir.name`) | ❌ Inconsistent |
| `tools/skills_tool.py` | `_find_all_skills()` | Uses **SKILL.md `name:` field** (`frontmatter.get("name", ...)`) | ✅ Correct |
| `hermes_cli/skills_hub.py` | `do_list()` | Compares using `skill["name"]` | ✅ Correct |

### Code Evidence

**skills_sync.py (Line 126):**
```python
skill_name = skill_dir.name  # ❌ Bug: uses directory name
```

**skills_tool.py (Line 558):**
```python
name = frontmatter.get("name", skill_dir.name)  # ✅ Uses name field
```

**skills_hub.py (Lines 523, 532):**
```python
name = skill["name"]
elif name in builtin_names:  # Never matches due to inconsistency
```

## Affected Skills

Skills where directory name differs from SKILL.md `name:` field:

| Directory | SKILL.md `name:` field | Wrong Class | Correct Class |
|-----------|----------------------|-------------|---------------|
| `audiocraft` | `audiocraft-audio-generation` | local | builtin |
| `gguf` | `gguf-quantization` | local | builtin |
| `modal` | `modal-serverless-gpu` | local | builtin |
| `peft` | `peft-fine-tuning` | local | builtin |
| `vllm` | `serving-llms-vllm` | local | builtin |
| `segment-anything` | `segment-anything-model` | local | builtin |
| `stable-diffusion` | `stable-diffusion-image-generation` | local | builtin |
| `lm-evaluation-harness` | `evaluating-llms-harness` | local | builtin |
| `trl-fine-tuning` | `fine-tuning-with-trl` | local | builtin |

## Impact

- Users see official builtin skills classified as `local` in `hermes skills list`
- `.bundled_manifest` uses directory names, but skill scanning uses `name:` field
- The comparison `name in builtin_names` in `do_list()` never matches for affected skills

## Reproduction Steps

1. Install Hermes Agent with bundled skills
2. Run `hermes skills list`
3. Observe that skills like `audiocraft-audio-generation` show as `local` instead of `builtin`

## Expected Behavior

All skills in `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/skills/` should be classified as `builtin` when listed.

## Suggested Fix

Update `tools/skills_sync.py` to read the `name:` field from SKILL.md instead of using directory name:

```python
def _discover_bundled_skills(bundled_dir: Path) -> List[Tuple[str, Path]]:
    skills = []
    for skill_md in bundled_dir.rglob("SKILL.md"):
        if "/.git/" in str(skill_md):
            continue
        skill_dir = skill_md.parent
        
        # Read name from SKILL.md frontmatter
        content = skill_md.read_text()[:4000]
        skill_name = None
        for line in content.split('\n'):
            if line.startswith('name:'):
                skill_name = line.split(':', 1)[1].strip()
                break
        if not skill_name:
            skill_name = skill_dir.name  # fallback
        
        skills.append((skill_name, skill_dir))
    return skills
```

## Workaround (Until Fixed)

Manually update `~/.hermes/skills/.bundled_manifest` to use SKILL.md `name:` field values instead of directory names:

```bash
# Wrong (directory name)
audiocraft:hash123

# Correct (SKILL.md name field)
audiocraft-audio-generation:hash123
```

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: Latest version from main branch
- OS: Ubuntu Linux
- Python: 3.x

## Additional Context

This bug affects any skill where the directory name differs from the `name:` field in SKILL.md frontmatter. The inconsistency between `skills_sync.py` and `skills_tool.py`/`skills_hub.py` causes the manifest-based classification to fail.

items.title: Hermes tool-calling pipeline can corrupt tool names and JSON arguments, causing generic tool-call failures

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

Hermes intermittently fails tool calls because malformed tool-call payloads reach the central validator in `run_agent.py`.

This is not limited to one tool. It affects the generic tool-call path and shows up across multiple tool names.

## Symptoms

Observed duplicated tool names include:

- `skills_listskills_list`
- `session_searchsession_search`
- `skill_viewskill_view`
- `web_searchweb_search`
- `execute_codeexecute_code`

Observed duplicated adjacent JSON argument payloads include:

- `{"category":"research"}{"category":"research"}`
- `{"a":1}{"a":1}{"a":1}`
- `{"name":"reddit-saas-idea-miner","file_path":""}{"name":"reddit-saas-idea-miner","file_path":""}{"name":"reddit-saas-idea-miner","file_path":""}`

Typical errors include:

- `Model generated invalid tool call: skills_listskills_list`
- `Tool 'skill_viewskill_view' does not exist. Available tools: ...`
- `Error: Invalid JSON arguments. Extra data: ...`

## Impact

- valid tools are rejected as invalid because their names are duplicated/mangled
- valid argument objects are rejected because duplicated adjacent JSON objects form invalid JSON
- Hermes can get stuck retrying/self-correcting instead of executing the intended tools
- in chat surfaces this can leave the session looking wedged or endlessly “typing”

## What I verified

Current upstream `main` on GitHub does not appear to contain the stronger duplicated-name / duplicated-JSON repair logic.

Verified against a fresh clone of:

- `https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent.git`

At the time checked:

- `main` HEAD was `1789c2699afb00f84e70b15a4dbbb6092a357ad1`

In that clean clone of `run_agent.py`:

- `_repair_tool_call(...)` exists, but only with:
  - lowercase repair
  - hyphen/space to underscore normalisation
  - fuzzy match
- the stronger helpers/markers were not present:
  - `_repair_duplicated_json_args(...)`
  - duplicated-name collapse for cases like `skills_listskills_list`
  - log marker: `Auto-repaired duplicated JSON arguments`

## Root cause

The issue appears to be malformed tool-call data arriving at the generic validation path in:

- `run_agent.py`

The tool registry itself is not the core problem:
- affected tools existed in the loaded tool definitions
- the failure was corruption of tool names / arguments before successful execution

## Proposed fix

Add central defensive repair in `run_agent.py` for two confirmed corruption modes:

### 1. Repeated tool-name repair

Examples:
- `skills_listskills_list` -> `skills_list`
- `skill_viewskill_view` -> `skill_view`
- `session_searchsession_search` -> `session_search`
- `web_searchweb_search` -> `web_search`

### 2. Exact duplicated adjacent JSON-argument repair

Examples:
- `{"category":"research"}{"category":"research"}` -> `{"category":"research"}`
- `{"a":1}{"a":1}{"a":1}` -> `{"a":1}`

Repair should be conservative:
- exact repeated payloads can be collapsed
- mismatched payloads should still fail safely

## Notes

This was reproducible in live use and not just in synthetic tests.

In addition to tool-call corruption, a stuck chat/typing state was also observed after a research run completed successfully in the session log, suggesting the bad tool-call/retry path may contribute to chat-facing sessions appearing wedged.

items.title: hermes model locks to first model on multi-model custom endpoints
items.body:
## Bug

When a user configures a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint with multiple models (e.g. OpenRouter, vLLM, or any provider serving 2+ models), `hermes model` locks to whichever model was picked first with no way to switch.

## Root cause

`_model_flow_named_custom()` in `hermes_cli/main.py` (L1700) checks if the `custom_providers` entry already has a saved `model` field. If so, it immediately activates and returns **without probing the endpoint or showing the selection menu**.

```python
if saved_model:
    _save_model_choice(saved_model)
    # ... activate ...
    print(f"✅ Switched to: {saved_model}")
    return  # <-- early return, no menu shown
```

On the first run, the user picks a model and it gets saved to `custom_providers[].model`. On every subsequent run of `hermes model`, the early-return fires and the user never sees the model selection menu again.

## Repro

1. Add a custom provider with multiple models:
   ```yaml
   custom_providers:
     - name: "My vLLM"
       base_url: "https://my-vllm.example.com/v1"
       api_key: "sk-..."
   ```
2. Run `hermes model`, select the custom provider, pick model A → works
3. Run `hermes model` again, select the same custom provider → immediately says "✅ Switched to: model-A" without showing the model list

## Expected behavior

`hermes model` should always probe the endpoint and show the model selection menu, with the current model pre-selected and marked `(current)`. If the endpoint probe fails, fall back to the saved model with an option to type a different name.

## Impact

Affects all users with multi-model custom endpoints (OpenRouter proxies, vLLM clusters, any OpenAI-compatible API serving >1 model).

items.title: delegate_task silently truncates batch tasks beyond MAX_CONCURRENT_CHILDREN
items.body:
## Bug

`delegate_task` in batch mode silently drops tasks beyond `MAX_CONCURRENT_CHILDREN` (hardcoded to 3):

```python
# tools/delegate_tool.py:559
task_list = tasks[:MAX_CONCURRENT_CHILDREN]
```

The model sends 5 tasks, gets results for 3, is never told 2 were dropped. No error, no warning, no indication in the response. The model assumes all 5 ran.

Additionally, the JSON schema has `"maxItems": 3` (line 923), which blocks the model from even attempting >3 tasks before the runtime could provide a useful error.

## Expected behavior

Either run all N tasks (possibly batching them), or return a clear error explaining the limit and how to fix it.

## Fix (PR linked)

- Replace silent truncation with a clear `tool_error` explaining the count, the limit, and how to configure it
- Make the limit configurable via `delegation.max_concurrent_children` in config.yaml (default 3)
- Remove `maxItems: 3` from the schema — the runtime check gives a much more actionable error
- Backwards compatible: default stays 3, existing configs unchanged

items.title: [Telegram] Second half of split long messages lost when batch delay window is too short
items.body:
## Problem

When a user pastes a long message into Telegram, the Telegram client splits it at ~4096 characters and sends it as multiple updates. Hermes has text batching (`_enqueue_text_event` at `telegram.py:2153`) that buffers rapid successive messages and concatenates them before dispatching.

However, the default batch delay is 0.6 seconds (`HERMES_TELEGRAM_TEXT_BATCH_DELAY_SECONDS`). If the second chunk arrives more than 0.6s after the first (slow network, large message, Telegram server delay), the first chunk is already flushed and dispatched. The second chunk then:

1. Arrives as a separate message
2. Gets queued behind the agent's in-progress response to the first chunk
3. Is never processed as part of the original message — the agent only sees the first half

## User report

User pasted a long response from another tool. The message was split by Telegram into two parts. Hermes only processed the first part and responded based on incomplete information. The second part was silently lost.

## Existing mitigation

The batching at `telegram.py:2153-2180` correctly handles the common case (chunks arriving within 0.6s). The issue is edge cases where chunks are delayed.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Increase default delay** — 0.6s may be too tight for large messages on slow connections. 1.0-1.5s would catch more splits with minimal latency impact.

2. **Character-aware batching** — if the first chunk is exactly ~4096 chars (Telegram's split point), wait longer for a continuation since a split is almost certain.

3. **Configurable per-user** — `HERMES_TELEGRAM_TEXT_BATCH_DELAY_SECONDS` is already an env var but users don't know about it. Document it in the Telegram setup guide.

## Info

- Telegram's message split point: 4096 characters
- Default batch delay: 0.6s (`HERMES_TELEGRAM_TEXT_BATCH_DELAY_SECONDS`)
- No max batch message count limit
- Code: `gateway/platforms/telegram.py:2153-2180`

items.title: [Gateway] Split inbound messages lost on Discord, Feishu, Matrix, WeCom — no text batching
items.body:
## Problem

When a user pastes a long message, the messaging client splits it at the platform's character limit. If the gateway doesn't batch these chunks, only the first part is processed and the rest is silently lost or processed as a separate message after the agent has already responded.

## Affected platforms

| Platform | Message limit | Has inbound batching? | Status |
|----------|--------------|----------------------|--------|
| **Discord** | 2000 chars | **No** | Worst — low limit, no batching at all |
| **Feishu** | ~4096 chars | Yes (0.6s static delay) | Has batching but no adaptive delay for splits |
| **Matrix** | 4000 chars | **No** | No batching |
| **WeCom** | 4000 chars | **No** | No batching |
| Telegram | 4096 chars | Yes (adaptive) | Fixed in PR #6891 |
| Signal | 8000 chars | No | Lower risk due to higher limit |
| WhatsApp | 65536 chars | No | Low risk |
| Slack | 39000 chars | No | Low risk |
| DingTalk | 20000 chars | No | Low risk |

## Impact

Discord is the most impacted — at 2000 chars, even a moderate code block or prompt gets split. Users pasting code, error logs, or long instructions will routinely lose the second half.

## Suggested fix

Port the adaptive batching pattern from the Telegram adapter (PR #6891):

1. Buffer rapid successive text messages from the same user/chat
2. Concatenate chunks before dispatching
3. Use adaptive delay: if the latest chunk is near the platform's message limit, wait longer (continuation is almost certain)
4. Flush when a short chunk arrives (end of the message)

The pattern is ~20 lines per adapter. Discord and Feishu are the highest priority.

## Progress

| Platform | Status | PR |
|----------|--------|----|
| Telegram | Fixed | #6891 — adaptive batch delay (21 lines) |
| Discord | Fixed | #6894 — text batching from scratch (66 lines) |
| Feishu | Has batching, needs adaptive delay | — |
| Matrix | No batching | — |
| WeCom | No batching | — |

## Ref

- `gateway/platforms/telegram.py:2153-2197` — batching code to port to remaining platforms

items.body:
## Original Request

> and another feature - instead of ENTER to sbumit new message and interrupt, maintain a queue like Cursor IDE, and only if user ENTER with empty mes
> sage, it enqueue mimedaitley, otherwais it will start

## Agent's Two Cents (could be wrong)

> Everything below is the AI agent's best guess based on the current codebase.
> Take with a grain of salt — the original request above is the only thing that came from a human.

**Suggested priority: p2**

### Problem / Motivation

Hermes CLI already supports interrupt-on-Enter, but that default is too trigger-happy for long-running work. The missing piece is a more natural, Cursor-style busy-input UX where users can keep drafting follow-ups without accidentally nuking the current run.

### What We Checked

- `cli.py` already has `display.busy_input_mode` with `interrupt` vs `queue` (`cli.py:1516-1518`).
- Busy Enter already routes to `_pending_input` in queue mode instead of `_interrupt_queue` (`cli.py:7659-7677`).
- `/queue <prompt>` already exists as an explicit manual fallback (`cli.py:4945-4955`).
- Docs already describe queue mode (`website/docs/user-guide/cli.md:216-231`).
- Tests already cover the current queue-vs-interrupt split (`tests/cli/test_cli_init.py:99-149`).
- Related open issues already exist around queueing and busy-input UX: #5504, #4772, #5057.
- Similar composition-first busy-input behavior also exists in Claude Code, so this is not just a Cursor-specific expectation.

### What still hurts

- The current queue support is config-driven and fairly hidden.
- Enter still feels semantically overloaded: submit, interrupt, or queue depending on state/config.
- There is no obvious Cursor-style or Claude Code-style "keep typing while busy, then explicitly send when ready" gesture.
- The requested empty-submit behavior is not implemented or documented.

### Proposed Solution

Add a CLI busy-input mode oriented around composition first, submission second:

- While the agent is busy, let the input box behave like a draft buffer by default, aligning more closely with workflows users already know from tools like Cursor IDE and Claude Code.
- Do **not** treat every Enter as immediate submit/interrupt.
- Support an explicit blank-submit gesture: when the user presses Enter on an empty trailing line (or otherwise signals an empty-message submit state), Hermes enqueues the drafted follow-up immediately.
- Keep `/queue` as an explicit command, but make the zero-friction keyboard path first-class.
- Preserve `interrupt` mode for users who prefer aggressive redirect behavior.

### Dependencies & Potential Blockers

No major blockers identified.

### How to Validate

- Start a long-running CLI task.
- Type a multi-line follow-up while the agent is still working.
- Press Enter inside the draft and confirm Hermes does **not** interrupt the current run prematurely.
- Trigger the blank-submit gesture and confirm the draft is queued exactly once.
- Confirm the queued prompt runs automatically after the active turn completes.
- Confirm `display.busy_input_mode: interrupt` still preserves current interrupt behavior.
- Confirm `/queue` still works.

### Best Validation Path

Run Hermes CLI with a deliberately long task, compose a follow-up during execution, and verify the full path manually: draft -> no interrupt on ordinary Enter -> blank-submit queues -> queued message runs after completion. Back this with focused CLI tests around the Enter handler and pending/interrupt queues.

### Best Human Demo

A short terminal recording is the best demo: show a long-running task, type a multi-line follow-up during execution, hit normal Enter without interruption, then use the blank-submit gesture and show the queued prompt firing after the current run finishes.

### Scope Estimate

medium

### Key Files/Modules Likely Involved

- `cli.py`
- `tests/cli/test_cli_init.py`
- `website/docs/user-guide/cli.md`
- potentially `hermes_cli/commands.py` if keybinding/help text needs surfacing

### Architecture Diagram

```text
User keyboard input
        |
        v
+-------------------+
| CLI input buffer  |
| draft composition |
+-------------------+
        |
        | Enter while busy
        v
+-----------------------------+
| Busy-input policy           |
| - interrupt                 |
| - queue                     |
| - cursor-style draft/queue  |
+-----------------------------+
      |                 |
      | interrupt       | enqueue
      v                 v
+-------------+   +----------------+
| interrupt   |   | _pending_input |
| _queue      |   | FIFO follow-up |
+-------------+   +----------------+
      |                 |
      v                 v
 active run stops   active run finishes
      |                 |
      +--------+--------+
               v
        next agent turn
```

### Rough Implementation Sketch

- Refactor the Enter handler in `cli.py` so busy-state submission policy is centralized instead of baked into a single immediate branch.
- Introduce a composition-oriented busy mode or sub-mode for blank-submit semantics.
- Track whether the current busy-state buffer ends in an empty line / explicit submit gesture.
- Add tests for single-line, multi-line, empty-line submit, and regression coverage for existing `interrupt` and `queue` modes.
- Document the behavior in CLI docs and config examples.

### Open Questions

- Should this be a brand-new mode (for example `draft_queue`) or an extension of existing `queue` mode?
- Should blank-submit mean “buffer ends with an empty line” or “cursor is on a blank line and Enter is pressed again”?
- Should there also be an explicit hotkey like Alt+Enter or Ctrl+Enter for immediate queueing, alongside the blank-submit gesture?

### Potential Risks or Gotchas

- Prompt-toolkit keybinding changes can get confusing fast if submit semantics differ too much between idle and busy states.
- Multi-line editing, slash commands, and pasted content can regress if the Enter routing becomes too clever.
- If the behavior is under-specified, users may accidentally queue drafts they thought were still being edited.

### Related Issues

- #5504 — feat: dual queue — follow-up (Alt+Enter) + steering (Enter/queue mode)
- #4772 — Feature request: Message queue for gateway (don't interrupt running agent)
- #5057 — Message handling behavior when multiple messages arrive during active agent execution

items.title: bug: credential pool _persist overwrites concurrent auth entries and _sync_codex_entry_from_cli rolls back exhaustion status

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
### Describe the bug

When using a credential pool with multiple entries for `openai-codex` (e.g. `device_code` and a manual second account like `chatgpt-2`), if the primary credential hits a rate limit (HTTP 429), the `_persist()` function in `CredentialPool` overwrites `auth.json` with only the in-memory entries of the current session, implicitly deleting any credentials that were added by other processes since the session started.

Furthermore, `_sync_codex_entry_from_cli()` attempts to resync the exhausted credential by reading `~/.codex/auth.json`. This mistakenly rolls back the `last_status` exhaustion marker and replaces the tokens with stale ones, causing the next request to fail with `401 Unauthorized`. 

When both bugs collide:
1. Primary hits 429.
2. `_persist()` saves exhaustion state but deletes the secondary credential from `auth.json` because it wasn't in the current `AIAgent` memory snapshot.
3. `_sync_codex_entry_from_cli()` un-exhausts the primary and replaces its tokens with stale ones.
4. Next request uses primary again, gets 401.
5. Primary is marked exhausted again.
6. Pool attempts to rotate, but the secondary credential is gone, leading to immediate fallback to another provider.

### To Reproduce

1. Start an interactive `hermes` session with `openai-codex` as the provider.
2. In another terminal, run `hermes auth add openai-codex --label chatgpt-2` and complete the device-code login.
3. In the first terminal, trigger a rate limit on the primary account (e.g. exhaust the usage limit).
4. Observe the console output: it fails to rotate to `chatgpt-2` and instead falls back to the next provider (e.g., `gemini`).
5. Run `hermes auth list openai-codex`. The `chatgpt-2` credential is gone.

### Expected behavior

1. `_persist()` should read `auth.json` from disk, update only the credentials present in memory (by ID), and merge them with any new credentials added by other processes, rather than blindly overwriting the provider's array.
2. `_sync_codex_entry_from_cli()` should immediately return if the credential source is manual (`_is_manual_source(entry.source)`), preventing stale CLI tokens from overwriting native Hermes OAuth tokens.

```text

- OS: Linux / macOS
- Provider: openai-codex
```

items.title: Background processes accumulate zombies; process tool reports dead processes as running
items.body:
## Bug

Background processes started with `terminal(background=true)` become zombies (`<defunct>`) when they exit. The `process` tool continues to report them as "running" because it tracks the wrapper PID without checking if it's a zombie.

## Reproduction

```
# Start several background processes with different durations
terminal("sleep 10", background=true)   # → PID 393
terminal("sleep 65", background=true)   # → PID 412
terminal("sleep 73", background=true)   # → PID 435
terminal("sleep 300", background=true)  # → PID 9

# Wait for the short ones to finish, then check:
process(action="list")
# Reports all 4 as "running" ✅

# But ps auxwww shows:
# PID 9    sleep 300     running ✅
# PID 393  [bash] <defunct>  zombie ❌
# PID 412  [bash] <defunct>  zombie ❌
# PID 435  [bash] <defunct>  zombie ❌
```

## Root cause

Two compounding issues:

1. **No zombie reaping.** The sandbox container's PID 1 is `sleep 2h` (from `docker run ... sleep 2h`), not an init process. It doesn't call `wait()` on orphaned children, so completed background processes become zombies instead of being reaped.

2. **`process` tool doesn't check process state.** `ProcessRegistry` tracks wrapper PIDs and reports them as "running" based on whether the PID exists, without checking `/proc/<pid>/status` for zombie state. A zombie PID still exists (it's in the process table until reaped) so the registry incorrectly reports it as alive.

## Expected behavior

- Completed background processes should be reaped (not zombie).
- `process(action="list")` should show completed processes as "exited" with their exit code.
- `process(action="poll")` on a completed process should return its final output + exit status.

## Possible fixes

1. **Use `--init` flag on `docker run`** (adds `tini` as PID 1) so orphaned children are reaped automatically.
2. **Have the process registry call `os.waitpid(pid, os.WNOHANG)` on poll/list** to detect and reap zombies.
3. **Both** — `--init` for the container-level fix, `waitpid` for the registry-level fix.

## Environment

- Docker backend (sandboxed containers)
- Container entrypoint: `sleep 2h` (not an init process)
- Hermes process registry: `tools/process_registry.py`

items.title: Feature: TTS Speed Control — Wire native rate params for Edge/OpenAI, add ffmpeg atempo fallback for NeuTTS/ElevenLabs
items.body:
## Overview

TTS speed/rate control is only wired up for MiniMax (`tts.minimax.speed`). The other four providers — Edge TTS, OpenAI TTS, ElevenLabs, and NeuTTS — all ignore any `speed` config. Users running local voice (especially via the TUI) have no way to speed up playback without manual post-processing. This is particularly painful for NeuTTS users who are deliberately trading cloud latency for local inference and want faster readback to compensate.

---

## Current State in Hermes Agent

### What works
- `tts.minimax.speed` is read at `tools/tts_tool.py:308` and passed to the MiniMax API as `voice_setting.speed`
- `voice.silence_threshold` and `voice.silence_duration` are configurable (and work well for input tuning)

### What doesn't work
- **Edge TTS**: `edge_tts.Communicate()` accepts a `rate` parameter (e.g. `"+50%"`) but `_generate_edge_tts()` at line 183 doesn't pass it — only `text` and `voice`
- **OpenAI TTS**: `client.audio.speech.create()` accepts `speed` (0.25–4.0) but `_generate_openai_tts()` at line 265 doesn't pass it
- **NeuTTS**: `neutts_synth.py` doesn't accept a `--speed` arg. NeuTTS may not support native speed control at the model level — needs investigation
- **ElevenLabs**: No native speed parameter in the API. Speed adjustment would require post-processing
- A top-level `tts.speed` or per-provider `tts.<provider>.speed` key placed in `config.yaml` is silently ignored for all providers except MiniMax
- No post-generation playback speed adjustment exists (ffmpeg `atempo` or similar)

### Config defaults (`hermes_cli/config.py:409-431`)
The `DEFAULT_CONFIG["tts"]` section has no `speed` key for any provider except (implicitly) MiniMax via its sub-dict. Edge, OpenAI, and NeuTTS sub-dicts have no `speed` field.

---

## Implementation Plan

### Tier 1 — Native speed params (trivial, covers Edge + OpenAI + MiniMax)

**Edge TTS** — pass `rate` to `Communicate()`:
```python
# tts_tool.py _generate_edge_tts()
edge_config = tts_config.get("edge", {})
voice = edge_config.get("voice", DEFAULT_EDGE_VOICE)
speed = edge_config.get("speed", 1.0)
# Edge TTS rate is a percentage string: "+0%" = 1.0x, "+50%" = 1.5x
rate_str = f"+{int((speed - 1) * 100)}%" if speed >= 1 else f"{int((speed - 1) * 100)}%"
communicate = _edge_tts.Communicate(text, voice, rate=rate_str)
```

**OpenAI TTS** — pass `speed` to `speech.create()`:
```python
# tts_tool.py _generate_openai_tts()
oai_config = tts_config.get("openai", {})
speed = oai_config.get("speed", 1.0)
response = client.audio.speech.create(
    model=model, voice=voice, input=text,
    response_format=response_format, speed=speed,
    ...
)
```

**MiniMax** — already works via `tts.minimax.speed`.

### Tier 2 — ffmpeg `atempo` fallback (covers NeuTTS + ElevenLabs + any provider)

For providers without native speed support, apply ffmpeg post-processing:
```bash
ffmpeg -i input.wav -filter:a "atempo=1.5" -y output.wav
```

`atempo` supports 0.5–100.0 (values >2.0 need chained filters: `atempo=2.0,atempo=0.9` for 1.8x). This should run after generation but before the file is returned to the caller.

A global `tts.speed` key would serve as the default for all providers. Per-provider `tts.<provider>.speed` overrides it. When the provider supports native speed (Edge, OpenAI, MiniMax), use native. Otherwise, fall back to ffmpeg atempo.

### Tier 3 — Streaming playback speed (future)

The ElevenLabs streaming path (`_speak_sentence` → `sounddevice.OutputStream`) plays PCM at a fixed sample rate. Adjusting playback speed there would require resampling the PCM buffer (e.g. via `scipy.signal.resample` or changing the `samplerate` param). This is more complex and can be a follow-up.

### Config shape

```yaml
tts:
  provider: neutts
  speed: 1.5          # Global default (all providers)
  edge:
    voice: en-US-AriaNeural
    speed: 1.5        # Override for edge (uses native rate param)
  openai:
    model: gpt-4o-mini-tts
    voice: alloy
    speed: 1.8        # Override for openai (uses native speed param)
  neutts:
    model: neuphonic/neutts-air-q4-gguf
    device: mps
    speed: 1.5        # Override for neutts (uses ffmpeg atempo)
  minimax:
    speed: 1.5        # Already works (native API param)
```

### Deliverables

- [ ] Add `speed` key to `DEFAULT_CONFIG["tts"]` (global default, `1.0`)
- [ ] Add `speed` key to each provider sub-dict in `DEFAULT_CONFIG`
- [ ] Wire Edge TTS `rate` param in `_generate_edge_tts()`
- [ ] Wire OpenAI TTS `speed` param in `_generate_openai_tts()`
- [ ] Add ffmpeg `atempo` post-processing fallback for NeuTTS and ElevenLabs
- [ ] Read global `tts.speed` as default, allow per-provider override
- [ ] Tests for speed config resolution and edge/openai parameter passing
- [ ] Document in `cli-config.yaml.example`

### Files affected

- `tools/tts_tool.py` — all five provider functions + speed resolution helper
- `hermes_cli/config.py` — `DEFAULT_CONFIG["tts"]` speed keys
- `cli-config.yaml.example` — document the new keys
- `tools/neutts_synth.py` — no change unless NeuTTS adds native speed support

---

## Pros & Cons

### Pros
- Covers 4/5 providers with minimal code (Edge + OpenAI are ~5 lines each)
- ffmpeg fallback makes speed universal, including future providers
- Global + per-provider override matches existing config patterns (e.g. `stt.provider` + `stt.local.model`)
- Directly improves local voice UX — the primary use case for NeuTTS users

### Cons / Risks
- ffmpeg is a runtime dependency (but already required for Edge TTS → Opus conversion)
- `atempo` values >2.0 need filter chaining — slightly more complex
- NeuTTS at high speed via atempo may sound robotic (pitch shifts). A proper solution would need NeuTTS model-level support

---

## Open Questions

- Does NeuTTS support a native speed/rate parameter at the model level? If so, passing it through `neutts_synth.py` would be better than ffmpeg post-processing
- Should streaming ElevenLabs playback support speed adjustment (Tier 3), or is file-based post-processing sufficient for now?
- Should the global `tts.speed` apply to streaming mode as well, or only to file-based TTS?

## Summary
Installing `hermes-agent[all]` on macOS arm64 / Python 3.11 does not currently resolve cleanly because the `matrix` extra allows a `matrix-nio[e2e]` line that conflicts with Hermes core HTTP deps.

## Environment
- macOS (Apple Silicon)
- Python 3.11
- Hermes Agent v0.6.0

## Relevant Hermes packaging
`pyproject.toml` currently declares:

```toml
matrix = ["matrix-nio[e2e]>=0.24.0,<1"]
```

## Concrete conflict
In the Hermes venv after update:
- `httpx 0.28.1` requires `httpcore==1.*`
- `httpcore 1.0.9` requires `h11>=0.16`

From `matrix-nio==0.24.0` wheel metadata:
- `Requires-Dist: h11 (>=0.14.0,<0.15.0)`
- `Requires-Dist: python-olm (>=3.1.3,<4.0.0) ; extra == "e2e"`

So the Matrix/E2EE path allowed by Hermes packaging cannot coexist cleanly with the Hermes core HTTP stack.

## Repro
1. Create a fresh Python 3.11 venv on macOS arm64.
2. Install Hermes Agent v0.6.0.
3. Attempt to install `.[all]`.
4. Resolver enters the Matrix dependency path and the install does not complete cleanly.

When I tried to force a compatible Matrix line manually:
- `matrix-nio==0.24.0` can satisfy the `python-olm>=3.1.3,<4` side
- but it still conflicts with Hermes core because it requires `h11<0.15` while Hermes core lands on `h11>=0.16`

I also observed that newer `matrix-nio` releases move toward `python-olm~=3.2`, which was additionally problematic to build on this machine, but the hard packaging bug here is the `h11` incompatibility.

## Expected
Either:
- the `matrix` extra is pinned to a known-good compatible Matrix stack, or
- the Matrix extra is temporarily removed/guarded from `all` until a compatible dependency set exists.

## Actual
`hermes-agent[all]` advertises an install path that is not currently dependency-consistent for Matrix/E2EE on this environment.

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

## Problem

The CLI response behavior is inconsistent:

- Sometimes the response streams in real-time (tokens appear 
  progressively) — this feels responsive and clear.
- Other times there is a silent pause of several seconds (or longer) 
  before the full response appears at once — during this period there 
  is zero feedback.

During the silent period, it is impossible to know:
- Whether the agent received the message
- Whether it is still processing
- Whether streaming stalled or the response is about to arrive

## Expected Behavior

When there is no streaming output for more than ~1-2 seconds after 
sending a message, show a visible indicator (spinner, blinking cursor, 
or "thinking..." text) so the user knows the agent is still working.

The indicator should disappear automatically once output begins 
or the response completes.

## Current Behavior

No feedback during silent processing periods. The terminal appears 
frozen. Users cannot distinguish between "agent is thinking" and 
"something went wrong".

## Additional Context

This is especially confusing when using slower models or when the 
agent is performing multi-step reasoning before producing any output. 
The inconsistency between streaming and non-streaming responses makes 
the experience unpredictable.

### Proposed Solution

## Proposed Solution

Maintain a persistent status bar at the bottom of the CLI that 
reflects the current agent state in real-time.

### State transitions

| State       | Display                        |
|-------------|--------------------------------|
| Idle        | ● Ready                        |
| Sent        | ⟳ Sending...                   |
| Processing  | ⟳ Thinking... (Xs elapsed)     |
| Streaming   | ⟳ Responding... (Xs elapsed)   |
| Done        | ✓ Done  (Xs)                   |
| Error       | ✗ Error — see above            |

### Behavior

- Status updates immediately when the user hits Enter (Sent)
- Transitions to "Thinking" once the request reaches the agent loop
- Transitions to "Responding" once the first token arrives
- Shows elapsed time in seconds so the user always knows 
  how long the current request has been running
- Transitions to "Done" with total elapsed time once the 
  response is complete
- Returns to "Ready" after a short delay (e.g. 2s)

### Implementation hint

A lightweight approach would be a background thread that 
renders the status line using ANSI escape codes 
(\r to overwrite the current line), updated every ~200ms. 
This avoids adding heavy dependencies and works in any terminal.

### Alternatives Considered

items.title: model_aliases should support context_length and max_tokens fields
items.body:
## Problem

When using `model_aliases` in `config.yaml` to define shortcuts for custom provider models, the `context_length` and `max_tokens` fields are not read or displayed when switching models via `/model <alias>`.

Example config:
```yaml
model_aliases:
  mymodel:
    model: "some-model"
    provider: custom:myprovider
    base_url: "https://api.example.com/v1"
    context_length: 204800
    max_tokens: 131072
```

When running `/model mymodel`, the Context always shows the default 128000 tokens instead of the configured value.

## Root Cause

The `DirectAlias` NamedTuple and `_load_direct_aliases()` function in `hermes_cli/model_switch.py` only extract `model`, `provider`, and `base_url` from the alias config, ignoring `context_length` and `max_tokens`.

## Proposed Fix

1. Add `context_length` and `max_tokens` fields to `DirectAlias` NamedTuple
2. Update `_load_direct_aliases()` to read these fields
3. Add these fields to `ModelSwitchResult` dataclass
4. In `gateway/run.py`, prefer `result.context_length` over `model_info.context_window`

## Use Case

This is especially useful for custom providers (like local LLM servers, enterprise APIs) where the model catalog is not available via `/models` endpoint.

items.title: [UX] Dangerous-command approvals should explain likely action and concrete risk in plain language
items.body:
## Original Request

> 用 /fr 现在遇到dangerous的情况让我们允许已经做的很好了，但是还有值得提高的地方：用LLM帮我们把这个command可能在干什么，有哪些具体风险，用用户能理解的话简介地解释一下。
> **English Translation:** `/fr` already does a good job handling dangerous-command approvals, but there is still room to improve: use an LLM to briefly explain, in user-friendly language, what the command is likely trying to do and what concrete risks it carries.

## Agent's Two Cents (could be wrong)

> Everything below is the AI agent's best guess based on the current codebase.
> Take with a grain of salt — the original request above is the only thing that came from a human.

**Suggested priority: p2**

### Problem / Motivation

The current approval UX stops at showing the raw command plus a short pattern-match reason like `recursive delete` or `shell command via -c/-lc flag`. That is better than nothing, but still asks normal users to mentally decompile a shell command and infer the real-world risk themselves.

For flagged commands, Hermes should explain the likely intent and concrete consequences in plain language before asking the user to allow it.

### What We Checked

- `tools/approval.py` already detects dangerous commands via `DANGEROUS_PATTERNS` and combines that with Tirith findings.
- Gateway approval payloads currently carry only `command` + combined `description`; the user-facing prompt is basically `Command Approval Required` + raw command + `Reason: ...`.
- Slack (`gateway/platforms/slack.py`), Telegram (`gateway/platforms/telegram.py`), and Discord (`gateway/platforms/discord.py`) all render the same thin explanation layer.
- There is already auxiliary-LLM logic in `tools/approval.py` (`_smart_approve`) for machine risk judgment, but that judgment is not turned into a concise human-facing explanation.
- Related issue #4067 improved approval UX around misleading `always`, but it did not address "what is this command actually doing?" in plain language.

### Proposed Solution

When a command is flagged for approval, generate an additional short explanation block for the user with an auxiliary LLM.

Show three things together:
1. the raw command,
2. the deterministic trigger reason(s) from regex/Tirith,
3. a concise natural-language explanation such as:
   - **Likely action:** restart the Hermes gateway service
   - **Why Hermes paused:** this command can stop a live service / overwrite a system file / run an arbitrary shell payload
   - **Concrete risk:** this could interrupt active chats, delete files, or change machine state in a way that is hard to undo

This explanation should be advisory only. It should not replace the deterministic approval gate.

### Dependencies & Potential Blockers

- Requires an auxiliary LLM client to be configured if we want rich explanations.
- No major architectural blocker; the bigger risk is UX quality and hallucinated over-explanations.

### How to Validate

- Trigger a known dangerous command such as `rm -rf /tmp/testdir` and verify the approval prompt includes:
  - raw command,
  - matched rule,
  - plain-language "likely action" summary,
  - concrete user-facing risk summary.
- Trigger a benign-but-flagged command such as `python -c "print('hello')"` in approval mode and verify the explanation does not catastrophize.
- Disable or break the auxiliary LLM path and verify Hermes falls back cleanly to the current static prompt.
- Verify Slack, Telegram, and Discord all show the explanation in a readable compact form.

### Best Validation Path

Run a gateway session locally with approvals enabled, execute one obviously risky command and one harmless false-positive-ish command, then inspect the approval prompts on at least one messaging platform plus the CLI path. The shortest reliable path is a focused test around `check_all_command_guards()` plus one platform snapshot test for prompt rendering.

### Best Human Demo

A before/after screenshot or short GIF of the same approval prompt is the best demo: first the current `Reason: recursive delete`, then the upgraded prompt with `Likely action` and `Concrete risk` in plain English.

### Scope Estimate

medium

### Key Files/Modules Likely Involved

- `tools/approval.py`
- `gateway/run.py`
- `gateway/platforms/slack.py`
- `gateway/platforms/telegram.py`
- `gateway/platforms/discord.py`

### Architecture Diagram

```text
terminal command
      |
      v
check_all_command_guards()  ---->  deterministic detection
      |                              - regex dangerous patterns
      |                              - Tirith findings
      |
      +---- if flagged ----> explanation builder
                              |  raw command + matched reasons
                              |  + aux LLM summary (best effort)
                              v
                        approval payload
                              |
                              v
                 gateway / CLI prompt renderer
                              |
                              v
            user sees: command + reason + likely action + risks
                              |
                              v
                     allow once/session/always/deny
```

### Rough Implementation Sketch

- Add a helper in `tools/approval.py` that asks the auxiliary LLM for a tiny structured explanation object, e.g.:
  - `likely_action`
  - `user_facing_risk`
  - `why_flagged`
  - optional `confidence`
- Keep the prompt strict and short; require concise JSON-ish output or another tightly bounded structure.
- Pass the explanation through the existing approval payload so platform adapters can render it.
- Update Slack/Telegram/Discord approval messages to show the explanation without turning the prompt into a wall of text.
- Fall back to the current behavior if the LLM is unavailable, times out, or produces junk.

### Open Questions

- Should the explanation be generated only for messaging platforms, or for CLI approvals too?
- Should the LLM summary be cached per command string during a session?
- Should we expose a config toggle like `approvals.explain_with_llm`?
- Should we show a confidence/disclaimer like `best-effort explanation` to avoid false certainty?

### Potential Risks or Gotchas

- The LLM can confidently misread shell syntax. If the UX sounds too authoritative, that is dangerous.
- Extra latency on the approval path could make the prompt feel sluggish.
- Long explanations will make mobile/chat approvals worse, not better. Keep it brutally concise.
- The explanation must never become the source of truth for authorization; deterministic guards still need to decide when approval is required.

### Related Issues

- #4067 — [UX] Tool approval UX: "always" label is misleading, timeout is not configurable

items.title: Feishu topic progress messages create new topics instead of staying in the original topic
items.body:
# Summary
In Feishu topic/thread conversations, Hermes currently splits a single interaction across multiple topics: the final answer usually returns to the original topic, but intermediate progress messages (tool progress, status updates, processing messages) can create new topics instead of staying in the original one.

# Expected behavior
When a user mentions Hermes inside an existing Feishu topic, the entire lifecycle of that request should remain inside that same topic, including:
- tool progress
- status updates
- processing/intermediate messages
- final answer

Hermes should not create additional topics during processing.

# Actual behavior
Observed behavior:
1. User mentions Hermes in an existing Feishu topic
2. Hermes starts processing
3. Intermediate/progress messages appear in newly created topics
4. Final answer appears back in the original topic

This causes one logical conversation to be split across multiple Feishu topics.

# Reproduction conditions
- Platform: Feishu
- Context: topic / thread / forum-style group conversation
- Trigger: mention Hermes inside an existing topic
- More visible when tool progress / status output is enabled

# Analysis
This looks like a Feishu topic/thread routing inconsistency between different outbound message paths:

- The final reply path appears to correctly bind the response back to the original topic.
- The intermediate progress/status path does not appear to use an equally strong topic-binding strategy, so Feishu treats those messages as new topic/thread entries.

In other words, Hermes seems to partially support Feishu topics for final replies, but not for the full execution lifecycle.

# Why this matters
For topic-based workflows, users expect the entire conversation to stay scoped to one topic. Creating extra topics during execution makes the conversation fragmented and hard to follow.

# Suggested fix direction
Please ensure that all outbound messages associated with a request originating from a Feishu topic use a consistent topic/thread routing strategy, not just the final answer. This should apply to:
- tool progress messages
- status updates
- intermediate processing messages
- final response

# Acceptance criteria
- Mention Hermes inside an existing Feishu topic
- Hermes processes the request without creating any new topics
- All intermediate and final messages stay inside the original topic
- Multi-turn follow-ups in the same topic remain stable and do not fork into new topics

# Temporary workaround
Disabling Feishu tool progress/output reduces the symptom, but does not solve the underlying issue.

items.title: [Bug]: Tool progress markers in SSE content corrupt model behavior over time (Open WebUI / OpenAI-compatible API)
items.body:
### Bug Description

The Hermes API server adapter (`/v1/chat/completions`) injects tool-progress markers like `` `⏰ list` `` directly into the SSE `delta.content` stream. OpenAI-compatible frontends like Open WebUI treat `delta.content` as the assistant's literal response text, so these markers become a permanent part of the stored assistant message and are sent back to Hermes (as the assistant turn) on every subsequent request.

After enough turns, the conversation history contains many assistant messages with embedded `` `⏰ tool_name` `` markers. Through in-context learning, the model starts treating these markers as the natural response format for this conversation. Eventually it generates the markers as plain text instead of issuing actual tool calls, then makes up a plausible-looking response describing what it would have done. The user sees what looks like a normal tool-using response, but no tool ever runs and underlying state is never modified.

Smaller / local models (e.g. a 26B Gemma running on llama.cpp) appear especially vulnerable because their tool-calling behavior is more easily overridden by strong in-context patterns.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Hermes to expose the API server adapter (`/v1/chat/completions`).
2. Connect Open WebUI (or any OpenAI-compatible frontend that captures `delta.content` into the assistant message) to Hermes.
3. Use a smaller open-weights model via llama.cpp / Ollama / similar (tested with `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q5_K_M.gguf` on llama.cpp, `--ctx-size 65536 --parallel 1`).
4. In a single chat, repeatedly use a tool that has visible progress markers (the cron tool is the easiest — `⏰`):
   - "List my cron jobs"
   - "Create a cron job that runs every 5 minutes and prints hello"
   - "Show me the jobs again"
   - "Change the schedule of that job to every 10 minutes"
   - …continue for ~10–15 turns
5. After enough turns, ask the agent to perform another action on the cron jobs (list, update, delete).


### Expected Behavior

Tool-progress markers should be a UI/visualization concern, not part of the stored assistant message content. The model should not see `` `⏰ list` `` text in its own past responses, so it cannot learn to imitate that pattern instead of issuing real tool calls.


### Actual Behavior

- The agent shows tool-progress markers in the chat (`` `⏰ list` ``, `` `⏰ update` ``, etc.) exactly as it did in earlier successful turns.
- The agent confidently reports success and may even quote specific values (job IDs, schedules, etc.).
- **No tool is actually called.** Underlying state files (`jobs.json`) are never modified, listing returns stale or hallucinated content.
- The session never recovers — every subsequent tool request behaves the same way.
- Starting a **new** chat in Open WebUI always works.
- Restarting the Hermes container sometimes appears to "fix" the same session but this is sampling variance, not a real fix; the broken session can resume failing on the next request.
- Inspecting the assistant messages directly in Open WebUI's "edit message" view confirms the markers are stored as literal text inside the message content, e.g.

  ```
  `⏰ list`

  I found one active cron job:
  ...
  ```

I then patched `cron/jobs.py`, `tools/cronjob_tools.py`, and `run_agent.py` to log every tool call, every `tool_progress_callback` fire, and the structure of the LLM's response (whether it has tool_calls, the content preview, etc.).

**Working session (1–2 messages of history), asking to list cron jobs:**

```
[2026-04-10T04:50:52.639916] [AGENT] tool_progress_callback fired (sequential): tool.started name=cronjob
[2026-04-10T04:50:52.640096] [TOOL] cronjob(action='list', job_id=None)
[2026-04-10T04:50:52.640286] [JOBS] load_jobs() JOBS_FILE=/opt/data/cron/jobs.json exists=True
```

**Broken session (~15 messages of history), asking to update a cron job's schedule:**

```
[2026-04-10T05:11:36.620086] [AGENT] RESPONSE: has_tool_calls=False, n_calls=0, content_len=328, content_preview='`⏰ update`\n\n`⏰ list`\n\nIch habe den Schedule des Jobs `cdaf68524204` auf `*/4 * * * *` aktualisiert, um das Intervall auf 4 Minuten zu ändern.\n\n**Verifizierung:**\n* **Job-ID:** `cdaf68524204`\n* **Sched'
```

The broken session returns **zero tool calls**. The visible `⏰` indicators are literal text in `assistant_message.content`, generated by the model imitating the marker pattern it has seen many times in past assistant turns. The "successful" status reported to the user is fully hallucinated — no tool ever runs and `jobs.json` is never modified.

There are no errors in `gateway.log` or `error.log`.

### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Operating System

Linux Mint 22.3

### Python Version

3.13.5 (in Docker)

### Hermes Version

0.8.0 (2026.4.8)

### Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`gateway/platforms/api_server.py`, in `_handle_chat_completions._on_tool_progress` (around lines 567–576):

```python
def _on_tool_progress(event_type, name, preview, args, **kwargs):
    """Inject tool progress into the SSE stream for Open WebUI."""
    if event_type != "tool.started":
        return
    if name.startswith("_"):
        return
    from agent.display import get_tool_emoji
    emoji = get_tool_emoji(name)
    label = preview or name
    _stream_q.put(f"\n`{emoji} {label}`\n")
```

`_stream_q` is the same queue that feeds the streaming `delta.content` chunks in `_write_sse_chat_completion`. Anything pushed onto it is sent to the client as part of the assistant's textual response. OpenAI-compatible frontends (Open WebUI, LobeChat, LibreChat, etc.) store this content verbatim and send it back as the assistant turn on subsequent requests.

The model then sees its own past "responses" containing both progress markers and real answers. With enough examples in context, in-context learning takes over and the model starts producing markers as text instead of issuing actual `tool_calls`. This is a well-known LLM phenomenon: strong in-context patterns can override system-prompt instructions, and smaller / less capable models are more susceptible.


### Proposed Fix (optional)

Tool progress should not be mixed into `delta.content`. Options in order of preference:

1. **Don't inject progress markers at all** in the API server adapter. Frontends that want progress visualization can use the structured `/v1/runs` event stream instead.
2. **Send progress as a separate non-content SSE event** (e.g. a custom `event:` line) that compatible frontends can display but won't store as message text.
3. **Strip injected markers from the assistant content** before returning the final `chat.completion` response, AND filter them out when reading conversation history from incoming requests. Most backward-compatible — markers can still appear in real-time during streaming, but won't pollute the stored history.

## Workaround

- Start a new chat in Open WebUI when the agent stops calling tools.
- Or manually edit the recent assistant messages in Open WebUI and remove the `` `⏰ tool_name` `` markers from the message content.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?
